newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil moves to dismantle telecoms giant.
newsitem.headline: Brazil moves to dismantle telecoms giant.

text.p: Brazil unveiled plans to dismantle state telecommunications company Telebras, Latin America's largest phone company, by dividing it into Baby Bell-like regional units ahead of privatisation.

In a bill sent to Congress on Thursday, the government outlined a blueprint for the country's new private telecommunications sector, which is expected to attract over $100 billion in investments in the next six years.
The bill also calls for an independent watchdog agency designed to guarantee a competitive business environment free from government intervention.

Communications Minister Sergio Motta said he envisioned Telebras breaking up into three to five regional blocs, each with enough market promise to attract bids from the world's leading phone companies.

Among the most coveted regions up for grabs are Brazil's southern and southeast regions - home to the sprawling metropolitan areas of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro - where most of the country's industry and wealth is concentrated.
Officials, however, are expected to require private investors to expand service into the Amazon and other remote regions of Brazil.

Dozens of international operators, including AT&T Corp., Sprint Corp. and France Telecom, are eyeing the bill's progress. Many of the firms are already vying for concessions in Brazil's B and B cellular service, which is being auctioned separately.
The reform-minded government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso hopes privatisation will revamp Brazil's unreliable and inefficient telephone system.

A domestic telephone line on the black market costs as much as $4,000 and can take weeks to install. Telebras offers new lines for about $1,000, but customers have to wait for at least a year. As a result, most Brazilians are forced to rent lines for up to $150 a month.
Brazil has a huge telephone backlog, a situation that is expected to worsen if the economy enters a period of fast-paced growth.

There are just 10.8 telephones per 100 people in Brazil, compared to 50 per 100 in the United States. The government says the only way to improve those numbers is to hand over the telecommunications sector to private operators.
The eagerly-awaited bill was welcomed by markets as it kicked off a long-overdue privatisation process.
"Before, the market was just speculating and now it is down on paper that the government indeed wants to privatise," said analyst Maxim Medvedovsky of Banco Icatu.

Brazil has lagged behind its neighbours in turning over its bulky telecoms sector to private hands. Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Peru are among Latin American nations whose governments have pulled out of the telephone business in recent years.
The government hopes Telebras will be fully dismantled and sold off by the end of 1998, but market analysts said that goal appears overly optimistic.
